For 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6: NBC reported the game had a 22.3 rating/38 share, with NBC 'estimating today that 72 million people watched all or part of it' (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/). This 72 million figure is explicitly a cumulative/unduplicated reach number (people who watched 'at least part' of the broadcast), not a simultaneous peak — confirmed by Wikipedia: 'It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). The actual average/peak-type simultaneous audience for that 1998 game was 35.89 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings), which with the 1998 US population (~275.85 million) would be about 13% — still higher than 9.5% but nowhere near 26.1%. ## Post

I just found out that if you end up in a mental institution, all your debts get cancelled 😭

## Research findings

Post claims admission to a mental institution causes all your debts to be cancelled. This is false in South Africa (author's location) and generally. In South Africa debt relief requires a formal High Court sequestration/insolvency process under the Insolvency Act 24 of 1936, not hospital admission — the process requires you to be at least 18 and mentally capable of making financial decisions, be unable to pay debts, prove benefit to creditors, and hand assets to a court-appointed trustee https://www.debtbusters.co.za/faqs/what-is-sequestration/ . Being declared mentally incapable would therefore hinder, not trigger, sequestration. Where mental-health protections exist they are a temporary pause, not cancellation: Scotland's Bankruptcy and Diligence (Scotland) Bill creates a mental-health moratorium pausing recovery action until six months after treatment finishes for people receiving crisis care https://www.scottishlegal.com/articles/pause-on-debt-recovery-for-people-with-mental-ill-health . In US/UK contract law, mental illness/medication makes a contract voidable, not void — law does not erase it on its own, you must affirmatively challenge it with medical evidence tied to signing date, until then debt is fully enforceable https://getoutofdebt.org/269757/signed-debt-while-medicated-pressured-do-i-still-owe-it . No source supports automatic cancellation of all debts upon psychiatric admission.

## Post

I just found out that if you end up in a mental institution, all your debts get cancelled 😭

## Research findings

Post claims admission to a mental institution automatically cancels all debts. No such automatic cancellation exists. Debts remain legally enforceable after psychiatric admission/commitment; mental illness alone is not a defense for not paying debts. Even in the UK, which has a formal Debt and Mental Health Evidence Form (DMHEF) process, StepChange states "It is rare that creditors write off debt just because of a DMHEF. But they may write off part of it" https://www.stepchange.org/debt-info/debt-and-mental-health-evidence-form.aspx and that creditors "might write off a debt if they do not think you can ever pay it" because of a long-term condition with proof from doctor/social worker https://www.stepchange.org/debt-info/debt-and-mental-health-evidence-form.aspx — i.e. discretionary, case-by-case, not automatic on institutionalization. US debt advice for mental-health crisis is to ask hospital billing for financial assistance, hardship programs and interest-free payment plans, not cancellation https://getoutofdebt.org/mental-health-crisis-debt. In South Africa, cancellation/write-off requires insolvency/sequestration court process, not hospitalization. Claim risks encouraging self-institutionalization for debt relief.
